Smoker's articles at Cooks.

B. Barr returned Wednesday morning from a trip west.
articles.summary: B. Barr returns from a trip west; Cook's sells smokers' articles.

articles.text: Northern Pacific bonds sold yesterday as follows: Common, 18⅝; preferred, 42⅜.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific bond prices.

articles.text: As will be seen by the new time table of the N. P. R. R. the train arrives from the east at 5:57 p. m., and from the west at 9:02 a m.
articles.summary: New Northern Pacific time table: train from the east at 5:57 p.m., from the west at 9:02 a.m.

articles.text: Our whole being was gladdened by an invitation to dinner yesterday at the Pyramid Park hotel. Mr. Boyd is running the hotel profitably, and deserves his patronage.
articles.summary: The editor dines at the Pyramid Park hotel, run by Mr. Boyd.

articles.text: Peter Book has discovered a new streak of clay that makes the best kind of cement, and intends working it this winter. He will also make a large number of pressed brick.
articles.summary: Peter Book finds new clay for cement and plans pressed brick.

articles.text: The report so generally circulated that Half-breed Jack and Jack-ass Bob were hung in Montana for horse stealing seems to have been incorrect. They are both now in jail in Miles City.
articles.summary: Half-breed Jack and Jack-ass Bob were not hanged, but are in jail at Miles City.

articles.text: The pleasantest dance that has ever been held in Medora took place last evening in Roberts & Co.'s hall. There was an unusually large attendance, and nothing occurred to mar the pleasure of the occasion.
articles.summary: A large, pleasant dance at Roberts & Co.'s hall.

articles.text: Any one wishing to subscribe for any papers or magazines published anywhere, can best serve their purpose by coming to the COW BOY office and getting our rates. Subscriptions taken for any paper in the world.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy office takes subscriptions for other papers and magazines.

articles.text: J. C. O'Brien, a prominent broker of Deadwood, was in Medora Sunday, on his way home from the east. He was in New York during the campaign, and gave a vivid description of many of its prominent features.
articles.summary: Deadwood broker J. C. O'Brien passes through Medora from New York.

articles.text: Deer are more numerous than usual this year, and large numbers are being killed in the vicinity of Medora. The evening train last Monday ran into a band of about a hundred a few miles west of here and killed two.
articles.summary: Deer are plentiful; the evening train hit a band of about a hundred and killed two.

articles.text: The man arrested and taken to Mandan by Bill Jones, for setting fire to the prairie, was given his liberty last week. He started for Glendive, and west of here was caught in the cold snap and badly frozen. He is supposed to have been crazy.
articles.summary: A man arrested for setting a prairie fire was released and then badly frozen west of Medora.

articles.text: M. G. Hall, assistant superintendent of the N. P. Express Co., was here Monday, arranging rates, etc., with the stage company. Mr. Hall is a thorough business man, and to him in a large measure is due the good working of the express line.
articles.summary: M. G. Hall of the N. P. Express Co. arranges rates with the stage company.

articles.text: A meeting to organize a school board and arrange preliminaries for a first-class school will, by request of those actively interested, be held in Roberts' hall to-morrow, Saturday evening, at 7 o'clock. All who wish to have a good school should turn out.
articles.summary: A meeting to organize a school board is called for Saturday evening at Roberts' hall.

articles.text: A. Young came near having a serious accident last week, owing to a cartridge sticking in his Winchester. In ramming it out, the cap came in contrct with the firing pin and the cartridge exploded, breaking the breech of the gun, but not harming Mr. Young.
articles.summary: A. Young's Winchester breech is broken by an exploding cartridge; he is unhurt.

articles.text: Of all trite subjects in this country, weather is the tritest. But we venture to say that no other country under the sun has been blessed with as beautiful fall weather as we have had up to a week ago. Then came snow, and last Saturday night it was twenty-four degrees below zero, and no one walking about town needed an overcoat. Wednesday a delightful chinook breeze struck us, sending the thermometer to fifty degrees above zero. In spite of this great change there has been no discomfort.
articles.summary: Fine fall weather ended with snow and 24 below on Saturday night, then a chinook brought 50 above on Wednesday.

articles.text: Again has the Medora stage smashed all records. The coach arrived here last Tuesday night just thirty-two hours and five minutes out of Deadwood. This is time never before dreamed of, and beats the best time in or out of Deadwood by any stage over any line nearly four hours. There was no attempt whatever to make extra time, and not a horse was over-driven. There is no possibility of any other stage line beating this time, and it will stand as a record, until on a race against time it is almost certain that the time of the Medora stage will go considerably under thirty hours.
articles.summary: The Medora stage makes a record run from Deadwood: 32 hours 5 minutes.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. LIVE STOCK RHYMES.
articles.text:
All the writers of the day
Put the cunning things they say
Into rhyme:
But the poets seem to think
That their dainty high-flown ink,
And their time,
Is better spent upon a dream,
Or some such other airy theme,
Than on beef;
But in this they are mistaken,
And for once I'll try to waken
The belief—
Indeed, the knowledge—that for so long
Has not broken into song;
That to meat
And it's heat,
Or caloric, I should say,
We're indebted for the play
And the very wit
That would ignore it.
All the men that move the world
Round their necks have always curled
Number sixteen collars.
Now it's meat that makes these necks,
Meat that's eaten down in pecks,
With an appetite that recks
Not of dollars.
David was a live stock man
And a greater race he ran
Than any since;
He did't mince
Matters much upon a lark,
And this fiery, kingly spark
Wrought sad ruin to Uriah,
He'd remorse enough to buy a
Place in the kindom come.
But beef
Was chief
Topic when I began,
And not the live stock man.
Now pork, and beef and mutton
Are not coarse, and gross, but on
The contrary quite the reverse.
Every silken line and terse
Woven into poet's theme,
Every flash and every gleam
Fresh from genius' richest dream,
All the lovely airy things
Born of brain on singing wings,
All conceits and sweetest thought,
Out of meat are deftly wrought,
Gastric juice and teeth between,
By man's physical machine.
—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Reprinted comic verse in praise of meat, from the N. W. L. S. Journal.

Lost from the Little Missouri round-up, one bay horse 5 years old, branded J on left shoulder and S on right flank; partly broken and very wild when he left; had picket rope around neck. Any one returning or giving information of him will receive the above reward.
W. N. THOMPSON & CO., Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: W. N. Thompson & Co. offer $10 for a bay horse lost from the Little Missouri round-up.

From my ranch on Little Missouri, ten miles south of Medora, the night of November 19, a dark sorrel mare, weighing about nine hundred pounds, left front knee stiff, white and red scar on left side, far back, brand M bar on left hip. Mare about nine years old. The finder will be paid for his trouble by leaving information leading to her recovery with me.
A. YOUNG, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: A. Young reports a dark sorrel mare strayed or stolen from his ranch on the night of November 19.

The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock or a proportionate reward will be paid for the return of any of them. The stock consists of the following horses:

One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder as advertised in our brand columns. Also one light sorrel pony, white legs and face and branded NC on left shoulder and triangle JP on right shoulder also as advertised in our brand columns.

articles.headline: Notice.
articles.text:
To prevent bulls running on the range during the winter, for the benefit of cattle men, I have established and fitted up a bull ranch on the Little Missouri. I will receive, care for and feed hay to all bulls given in my charge for the sum of $2 per month per bull. The bull round-up started on Monday, November 18th, 1884, and all bulls will be received at the Royal Chambord ranch.
For further particulars apply to Pierre Wibaux, Royal Chambord ranch. Postoffice address, Mingusville, Dawson county, Dakota.
PIERRE WIBAUX.
articles.summary: Pierre Wibaux opens a winter bull ranch on the Little Missouri at $2 per bull per month.

articles.headline: Notice.
articles.text:
To whom it may concern:
The partnership heretofore existing between Gustave Grisy and Pierre Wibaux, under the firm name of Grisy & Wibaux, has been dissolved, dating from the 1st day of November, 1884. Pierre Wibaux is now the sole proprietor of the Royal Chambord cattle ranch, situated on Beaver Creek; also of the bull ranch situated on the Little Missouri. Pierre Wibaux assumes all the indebtedness of the late firm up to November 1, 1884. All persons having accounts will please present them at their earliest convenience.
PIERRE WIBAUX.
November 20, 1884.
articles.summary: Dissolution of the Grisy & Wibaux partnership; Pierre Wibaux becomes sole owner of the Royal Chambord ranch.

articles.text: Andy Williams was recently convicted of cattle stealing at Miles City. He has not yet been sentenced.
articles.summary: Andy Williams convicted of cattle stealing at Miles City.

articles.text: A meeting of the Shonkin and Highwood horse association, is announced to be held at Fort Benton, Mont., on the 29th.
articles.summary: Shonkin and Highwood horse association to meet at Fort Benton.

articles.text: The average weight of cattle now slaughtered is a third more than it was half a century ago.—[Stock Growers' Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping on heavier slaughter cattle.

articles.text: Probably the last shipment of range cattle for the season left Miles City Sunday. They were prime beef, and belonged to T. J. Bryan.
articles.summary: The season's last range-cattle shipment leaves Miles City.

articles.text: From present indications there seems to be no doubt that inside of two years all the stock ranges on the Little Missouri will be taken up.
articles.summary: Prediction that all Little Missouri ranges will be taken up within two years.

articles.text:
During the past few months the value of American live stock exported has aggregated a sum in excess of a million and a half dollars per month.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The market east is still overstocked with wool and has been this entire year, and notwithstanding this the country has paid more than $20,000,000 for foreign wools in the past twelve months.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Mr. W. J. Marsh, of Sheridan Navada, writes the National Live Stock Journal, of Chicago, that the blackleg is making fearful ravages in Nevada. He says that it will probly sweep the entire Pacific coast, and that it is liable to last for two years.

Of the 450,000 head of cattle shipped north by rail this year from Texas, 300,000 steers were under two years. There were few of the mammoth cattle of former years among them, which show shippers are beginning to realize that steers weighing from 1,000 to 1,200 pounds, market better in lots than the larger ones.—[Col. L. S. Record.

Before this last contagious disease boomers of Government officials "appointed because of supposed competency," etc; we admitted that pleuro-pneumonia did exist in isolated cow stables in the east. This admission was based on the reports of veterinarians who had "axes to grind," and now we defy any man to prove that there is a single case of contagious pleuro-pneumonia in the United States.—[Drovers' Journal.

The Breeders' Journal says that the demand for Herefords in America was never so urgent as it is to-day. There is scarcely a thoroughbred bull that is old enough for service in the hands of the breeders. The grade bull breeders are in the same position. The supply of both is exhausted and there is a probability that cattlemen on the plains will be contracting in advance for the next year.—[Stock Growers' Journal.

A recent dispatch sent out from Kansas City says that the committee appointed by the National Bureau of Animal Industry, to gather statistics of the cattle interests in the west, has nearly concluded its work. It is said that the report will show that there are about 25,000,000 head of cattle in the states west of the Mississippi river, being a gain of 30 per cent, since 1880. Texas leads with a gain of nearly 70 per cent.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.

The demand for thoroughbred bulls in western Colorado and by our farmers along the foothills will be greater this next season than it has ever been before. But they must come with well-authenticated pedigrees, when they will command good prices. Every known family of cattle have their admirers here, and every variety will here sell. A hundred-dollar bull will not bring five hundred, but he will command his full value and sell quick in the coming spring.—[Col. L. S. Record.

According to the National Stockman, the following is the receipt for the "government" harness dressing: "One gallon neat's foot oil, two pounds bay berry tallow, two pounds beeswax, two pounds beef tallow. Put the above in a pan over a moderate fire. When thoroughly dissolved, add two quarts of castor oil; then while on the fire, stir in one ounce of lampblack. Mix well, and strain through a fine cloth, to remove sediment, let it cool, and you have as fine a dressing for harness or leather of any kind as can be had."

It seems to us that cattle growers might increase their herds very materially by arranging to wean the calves in the fall. The usual custom is to mark, brand and turn them with the herd. Some cows will wean their calves, while others will not. Heifers are most apt not to wean their first calves. They seem to become attached to them and allow them to suck as long as they choose. Often we have seen yearlings on the range with their mothers, taking the milk of a younger calf. In early spring before the green grass comes, new-born calves who have to divide with yearlings generally get a small allowance, and are therefore stunted in their growth. Cattle owners should secure lands and inclose pastures in which to wean calves. They will find that by so doing their cattle will grow larger, and it is large steers that make the best beeves and bring top prices in the market. We heretofore suggested the advisability of keeping the range bulls in pastures at certain seasons of the year, and the same pastures would answer for weaning calves. Herd owners will have to do this, and the sooner they begin the better it will be for the improvement and increase of their cattle.—[Rocky Mountain Husbandman.
articles.summary: Range and livestock clippings from stock journals (exports, wool, blackleg, Texas cattle, pleuro-pneumonia, Herefords, cattle census, bulls, harness dressing, weaning calves).

Ready-print inside page: national editorial paragraphs under a Cow Boy heading, 'The Pith of the News' wire digest, 'Dakota Territorial News', poetry and serial fiction ('A Laconic Wooer', 'A Genuine Love Story').

articles.text: Bob Roberts of Medora, well known in Bismarck, shot but did not kill Geo. Heywood, who, had, it is claimed, threatened to kill him.
articles.summary: Item in the ready-print 'Dakota Territorial News' column: Bob Roberts of Medora shot George Heywood.

Ready-print inside page: speech by Mr. Blaine, 'The Hot Spell in Pike County', 'Under Flood Rock' and sugar-cane fiction/miscellany, and patent-medicine and mail-order ads (Cuticura, Allen's Lung Balsam, Hostetter's Bitters, Tutt's Pills, St. Jacobs Oil, Kidney-Wort, 'The Civil War' Century series).

articles.text:
Stationery at Cooks.

George Heywood's wound is healing kindly.
articles.summary: George Heywood's wound is healing.

articles.text: Bob Roberts returned Monday night from Bismarck.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts returns from Bismarck.

articles.text: C. W. Sleeper started for the Hills Monday morning on a business trip for the stage line.
articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper leaves for the Black Hills on stage-line business.

articles.text: Our list has been increased this week by twenty-three new subscribers. "It's on account of our winning way."
articles.summary: The Cow Boy gains 23 subscribers this week.

articles.text: Dr. Jorgens reports business as far better than he expected, and is greatly pleased at his choice of Medora as a home.
articles.summary: Dr. Jorgens reports good business in Medora.

articles.text: Oats along the N. P. R. R. are and for some time will be steady at 72 to 75 cents. In the Hills they are $2.50 and rising.
articles.summary: Oat prices along the railroad and in the Black Hills.

articles.text: Pat O'Hara has a gun for sale that he will guarantee, as he is acquainted with its pedigree. He says he has known it ever since it was a pistol.
articles.summary: Joke about Pat O'Hara's gun for sale.

articles.text: The N. P. R. R. Co., through B. Barr, has exchanged a number of stock calves and cows to the Custer Trail Cattle Company and Thompson & Co. for fine beeves.
articles.summary: The N. P. R. R. Co., through B. Barr, trades stock calves and cows for beeves with the Custer Trail Cattle Co. and Thompson & Co.

articles.text: Bob Roberts, while in Bismarck, gave away the town pet, Nellie, the cinnamon bear. There is liable to be an uprising of the citizens when the time comes for her shipment.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts gives away Nellie, Medora's pet cinnamon bear.

articles.text: Frank Howard, of Spearfish, was here Sunday, having come in from work on the stage line. Frank is one of the best and [fastest?] carpenters in the Hills, and is kept constantly busy.
articles.summary: Spearfish carpenter Frank Howard in Medora after work on the stage line.

articles.text: "Mike" is again officiating at John Warn's suburban retreat, alias the "oyster grotto." His recent political experience was disastrous, although it is currently reported that he beat Mr. S. for the postoffice.
articles.summary: "Mike" back at John Warn's oyster grotto after a political defeat.

articles.text: Sam English is getting to be a great psalm-singer. Since Wednesday night he has been singing "Unto us a child is born," but sticks on the next line, "Unto us a son is given" for it's a girl. Great is the thanksgiving in the house of English.
articles.summary: A daughter born to Sam English on Wednesday night.

articles.text: Dr. H. M. Jorgens has gone to Cav[e?] Hill, on the stage road, to spend Thanksgiving at John Arrington's ranch. He will probably bring his family with him on his return. Mr. Martin will continue to hold down the drug store during the doctor's absence.
articles.summary: Dr. H. M. Jorgens goes to John Arrington's ranch for Thanksgiving.

articles.text: A petition for the establishment of a school was circulated yesterday by Messrs. Coleman and Riley, and enough money subscribed to guarantee its opening. Dan Williams will be teacher, and the school will open next Monday morning at the Cantonment.
articles.summary: School petition circulated; school to open Monday at the Cantonment with Dan Williams as teacher.

articles.text: Trips to all points up and down the road and to the Hills have thoroughly convinced us that "there's no place like home." There is not a place on the N. P. R. R. or in the Hills that in proportion to its size is anywhere near as prosperous as Medora. "We're little, but oh, my!"
articles.summary: Editor boasts of Medora's prosperity.

articles.text: The work on J. D. Garver's store is nearly finished, and he will soon move in. Mr. Fisher is so well pleased with his building plans that he contemplates the building of other store rooms and possibly a roller rink. From the present popularity of this sport the rink would be a success.
articles.summary: J. D. Garver's store nearly done; Mr. Fisher plans more store rooms and perhaps a roller rink.

articles.text: Dan Friedman has gone to Cold Springs, Minn., to spend the winter and engage cattle for next season's contracts. We alluded some time ago to his having a superfluity of side-saddles, and as he left the extra one behind, it is a very supposable case that on his return the boys will all "smile."
articles.summary: Dan Friedman goes to Cold Springs, Minn., for the winter to engage cattle.

articles.text: It has been found that no petition for the organization of the county is on file, and no further move towards organizing can be made until this preliminary is arranged. The governor is anxious to have the matter settled, and will appoint the third commissioner on the arrival of the petition. To this end we have drawn up the petition, and have it in the COW BOY office. All residents of the county, tributary to Medora, are requested to sign it, and it will then be forwarded to [Belfield?], or a second one will be gotten up there. Those desiring a speedy organization will come in and sign.
articles.summary: A county organization petition is at the Cow Boy office for residents to sign.

articles.text: George Fitzgerald began Tuesday to excavate foundations for a large hotel on the corner of Third avenue and Third street. The dimensions of the building are to be [32?]x80, with the front on Third avenue looking south. The plan of the building is an exact model of the Merrill house at Glendive, and will be built in the most substantial manner. It will first be built of wood and then veneered with brick. J. C. Williamson has the contract for the carpenter work, and Peter Book for the brick work. The contractors are guarantees of the substantial nature of the work. When completed it will be the finest hotel between Miles City and Mandan.
articles.summary: George Fitzgerald begins foundations for a large hotel at Third avenue and Third street.

articles.text:
Cigars and tobacco at Cooks.

The Marquis returned last night from St. Paul.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Morès returns from St. Paul.

articles.text: Operator Ives, of Sentinel Butte, came up last evening to attend the Thanksgiving ball.
articles.summary: Operator Ives of Sentinel Butte comes for the Thanksgiving ball.

articles.text: Mrs. John Kiefer is still in Minnesota and not much improved in health. It is to be hoped that she will soon recover and return to Medora.
articles.summary: Mrs. John Kiefer still ill in Minnesota.

articles.text: Mike Coleman rounded up his family Tuesday, and found an unbranded member that had put in an appearance. It is not a maverick, however, and Mike now has its name on the tally sheet when the family is corralled for the night.
articles.summary: A child born to Mike Coleman on Tuesday.

articles.text: The plan for the brick work on George Fitzgerald's new hotel is a work of art, and would be no discredit to a railroad draughtsman. It was drawn by Peter Book and Henry Brick, who, as will be seen in the change in the brick yard advertisement, are prepared to do any work of this kind.
articles.summary: Peter Book and Henry Brick draw the brick-work plan for Fitzgerald's hotel.

articles.text:
Freighters Attention!

Confectionery of all kinds at Cook's store.
